qs.q: A patient is treated with ivermectin for onchocerciasis. The drug works by causing paralysis of the microfilariae. What is the primary mechanism of action?
o: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the junction
Inhibition of fatty acid biosynthesis pathway
Blockade of sodium channels in the nerve
qs.e: Ivermectin binds to glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing hyperpolarization and paralysis of the microfilariae.

qs.q: Black flies of the genus Simulium are implicated in onchocerciasis. What is their preferred larval breeding site?
o: Stagnant and polluted urban water body habitats
Clean and artificial container water sources
Brackish and coastal tidal pool environments
Deep and anaerobic swamp water locations
qs.e: Simulium larvae require fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water, typically found in mountain streams or rapids.

ai.title: Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Onchocerciasis is a filarial infection transmitted by black‑fly bites, causing skin disease and progressive ocular damage. Diagnosis relies on skin snips and clinical signs; ivermectin is the mainstay of treatment and community‑wide control.

sections.p: Onchocerciasis is a chronic filarial disease endemic to riverine areas of sub‑Saharan Africa and some Latin American foci. It presents with pruritic skin lesions, subcutaneous nodules and, if untreated, irreversible blindness.
b: Caused by the nematode Onchocerca volvulus
Most common in low‑resource, river‑valley communities

sections.p: Onchocerca volvulus is a long, thread‑like nematode. Adult worms live in subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) and release microfilariae that migrate through skin and eye tissues.
b: Adult worms: 30–50 cm, live up to 15 years
Microfilariae: 0.2 mm, migrate in dermis and ocular tissues
Endosymbiotic Wolbachia bacteria trigger much of the inflammatory response

sections.p: Infected black‑flies ingest microfilariae while feeding. In the fly, they develop to infective L3 larvae, which are transmitted to humans during subsequent bites.
b: Human → L3 inoculation → nodules → microfilariae release

sections.p: Clinical disease is staged by skin and ocular involvement. Early disease is pruritus and dermatitis; later, onchocercomas and ocular lesions lead to visual loss.
b: Acute: intense itching, papular rash, “sow‑sow” skin
Chronic skin: depigmentation (leopard skin), atrophy, nodules
Ocular: punctate keratitis → sclerosing keratitis → blindness

sections.p: Diagnosis combines clinical suspicion with parasitological confirmation. In low‑resource settings, skin snip microscopy is the cornerstone; serology and ocular examination add support.
b: If skin snip unavailable, rely on clinical triad (itching, nodules, visual symptoms) and epidemiology.

t.b: Does the patient have microfilariae in the dermis? Positive smear confirms active infection.
Are there characteristic corneal opacities or retinal changes? Findings support ocular onchocerciasis.
Is there exposure to O. volvulus? Useful for mapping; a positive test suggests infection but cannot confirm active disease.

sections.p: Ivermectin kills microfilariae and temporarily suppresses transmission; repeated dosing is required because adult worms persist. Community‑directed treatment (CDTI) is the WHO strategy.
b: Ivermectin 150 µg/kg PO every 6‑12 months – kills microfilariae, reduces ocular inflammation
Surgical excision of large onchocercomas only if causing obstruction

t.b: Will the patient develop fever, pruritus, lymphadenopathy after ivermectin? Indicates rapid microfilarial death; treat symptomatically.
Is the patient pregnant? Ivermectin is contraindicated in the first trimester; defer treatment until after delivery.

sections.p: Focus on the clinical pattern, epidemiology and the role of ivermectin. Remember the Mazzotti reaction and the need for repeated dosing.
b: Key clue: river‑valley residence + severe itching + palpable subcutaneous nodules
Never give diethylcarbamazine (DEC) in onchocerciasis – can cause severe ocular damage
In co‑endemic areas (Loa loa), watch for high Loa loa microfilaraemia before ivermectin

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden visual loss or eye pain
Severe systemic Mazzotti reaction with high fever, hypotension
Signs of secondary bacterial infection of nodules

faq.q: Why is DEC contraindicated in onchocerciasis?
faq.a: DEC rapidly kills microfilariae in the eye, causing intense inflammation and possible blindness.

faq.q: What is the purpose of doxycycline in onchocerciasis?
faq.a: It eliminates Wolbachia, sterilising adult worms and providing a macrofilaricidal effect.

faq.q: How often should community‑directed ivermectin be given?
faq.a: Every 6‑12 months, depending on transmission intensity, to keep microfilarial loads low.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer from a riverside village presents with severe itching and a palpable nodule on the thigh – what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform a skin snip microscopy to look for microfilariae; if unavailable, base decision on clinical triad and epidemiology.

How does ivermectin differ from DEC in its mechanism and safety profile for onchocerciasis? — Ivermectin paralyzes microfilariae via glutamate‑gated chloride channels; DEC kills microfilariae rapidly causing ocular inflammation, thus contraindicated.

A patient on ivermectin develops fever, rash and lymphadenopathy – what does this indicate and how should you manage it? — This is a Mazzotti reaction; treat symptomatically with antihistamines and NSAIDs, continue ivermectin schedule.
In a co‑endemic area with Loa loa, what precaution must you take before giving ivermectin? — Screen for high Loa loa microfilaraemia (>30,000 mf/mL) to avoid severe encephalopathic reactions.

Why might a patient with onchocerciasis still develop new nodules despite regular ivermectin? — Ivermectin only kills microfilariae; adult worms persist. Consider adding doxycycline to target Wolbachia.
What ocular findings are pathognomonic for onchocerciasis? — Punctate keratitis and sclerosing keratitis progressing to corneal opacities; fundus may show chorioretinal atrophy.

Explain the public‑health rationale for community‑directed treatment (CDTI). — Annual mass ivermectin reduces community microfilarial load, interrupting transmission without needing individual diagnosis.
A pregnant woman in the second trimester presents with onchocerciasis – what is the safest management? — Defer ivermectin until after delivery; provide symptomatic relief and monitor ocular status.
